book: 048 - The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations

chapters.file: ch28 - A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”.md
chapters.relation: Writing as a Yankees fan, Konig asks what makes a championship worth wanting: after Schopenhauer's picture of endless striving as suffering, he brings in Richard Taylor (meaning lies in the activity itself, never its completion) and then Nietzsche's will to power, which seeks worthy resistance to overcome. Thought experiments—a childhood 'big game' that turns out to be tee-ball, and the 2004 Sox trouncing the minor-league Atlantic League—show a title without worthy opposition is hollow. Hence the Yankees' twentieth-century dominance would mean nothing without the Red Sox as the sustained, worthy enemy (Bucky Dent, the Pedro-Zimmer melee, the 2004 ALCS collapse included).

chapters.file: ch29 - What Makes the Red Sox Great Is More than the Team.md
chapters.relation: Ulatowski argues the 'We Believe' motto is religious: Red Sox fandom is the a priori conviction that Boston is the sports city 'than which none greater can be conceived,' transplanting Anselm's ontological argument—necessary, contingent and impossible objects, existence as a perfection—to the Red Sox via Oliver Wendell Holmes's 'hub of the universe.' He rejects the parallel New York argument because it smuggles a posteriori championship counts into an a priori proof, and answers the fallacy-of-division worry by making Boston's greatness and the Red Sox's greatness an identity rather than a whole-to-part inference.

chapters.file: ch30 - Are These World Series Champions Really Our Red Sox.md
chapters.relation: Lee casts pre-2004 fandom as a Kierkegaardian leap of faith ('We Believe') and the Curse of the Bambino as Schopenhauer's irrational deterministic will, with the 1918–2004 cycle of spring hope and October collapse as Camus's Sisyphus. But he argues fans are really existentialists: blaming losses on fate or the Curse is Sartrean bad faith that evades responsibility, since fans did hold Bill Buckner (1986 error) and Grady Little (leaving a spent Pedro in during 2003 ALCS Game 7) individually accountable. The 2004 and 2007 champions remain 'our' Red Sox because we freely choose to care about the team's journey, not because it has a fixed essence; a coda borrows Russell's point about ambiguous reference for the word 'Yankee,' and Andy Wasif's appendix runs Yankees-as-evil through relativism, objectivism and subjectivism.

chapters.file: ch31 - V - Views from the Grandstands.md

chapters.relation: Macomber explains fan judgment through Kant's determinate judgment—subsuming sensuous particulars (white sphere, red stitches) under the concept 'baseball'—then warns, with Horkheimer and Adorno's 'disenchantment of the world,' that reducing careers to single concepts (Buckner = 'error,' Dave Roberts = 'The Steal,' Damon = 'traitor') negates everything else a player did, which is why Damon is booed at Fenway while Nomar received a standing ovation. Retired numbers like Jim Rice's 14 invert the process: the harshest reduction becomes an invitation that demands the player's story be told, magnifying rather than erasing him.

chapters.file: ch33 - Tie Goes to the Runner.md
chapters.relation: St. Martin runs the Fenway 'pink hat' controversy through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the virtuous fan is the mean between the deficient bandwagoner who waves at NESN cameras mid-pitch and the excessive diehard who memorizes Dice-K's ERA to belittle others. Terry Francona's courage in sending Dave Roberts in the 2004 ALCS (versus a reckless Ortiz steal attempt) illustrates virtue as the mean between cowardice and foolhardiness, and Aristotle's contrast between the love of honor and the love of contemplation shows both pink hatters and stats-obsessed diehards err by making fandom about themselves. She concludes that accepting fans in any color hat is the truly virtuous mean.

Goldwater reads Bill James's sabermetric revolution through Quine: science is a continuation of common sense, but mature science replaces the 'animal sense of similarity' (being a Yankee, batting average, RBI) with predictive, league- and park-adjusted categories, turning atomistic box-score tallies into holistic statistics that acquire meaning only from the whole web of data. Because science recognizes only repeatable types, it cannot countenance miracles—Carlton Fisk's 1975 homer greeted by the 'Hallelujah Chorus,' Dave Roberts's steal in 2004—whose meaning lies in happening exactly once. His resolution: GMs like John Henry and Theo Epstein need Quinean prediction, while fans keep the religious language of faith, hope, and redemption.

chapters.file: ch35 - Tearing Down Fenway Now That Would Be Offensive.md
chapters.relation: Mathis argues fans' contempt for ticket resellers is not about being overcharged, since resellers only charge what Fenway's scarcity market will bear. Following Rawls's A Theory of Justice, he treats access to Red Sox tickets as a public good deliberately sheltered from the free market by the random online waiting room, the five-year season-ticket list, baseball's antitrust exemption, and the 1924 Massachusetts anti-scalping law—all of which promote egalitarian access and a sense of community. Reselling offends because it exploits for private profit a good we collectively protect from market forces, as tearing down Fenway itself would.

Auxier's rhapsodic essay channels Bart Giamatti ('the Philosopher') on baseball as sacred leisure and uses Pythagoras—everything is Number, each thing's essence an unnamed ratio—to argue the sacred geometry of Fenway cannot be reduced to the dimensions of mere space. He casts the scorecard-keeping quantifiers (Steinbrenner, the Mathematikoi) against the meaning-seeking true believers (Giamatti, the Akousmatikoi), and claims the Yankees' demolition of their own temple, not the 2004 comeback, is what truly lifted the Curse of the Bambino and guarantees Boston will never tear down Fenway. It ends with circular time: the season, like the Babe finishing his career in Boston, always comes home.

chapters.file: ch37 - VI - So Good! So Good! So Good!.md

chapters.relation: Lee reads Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting as a Daoist skill story from the Zhuangzi: 'get a good ball to hit' matches the cicada-catcher's total absorption in the cicada's wings, hitting 'by feel' like the carpenter's hammer matches Cook Ding carving without looking, and Williams's midnight batting practice after Korea matches the wheelwright grown old at his craft—effortless spontaneity produced by disciplined practice and unified attention, not mere mechanics. Williams's 'proper thinking' is Daoist sorting of objective conditions rather than abstract disputation. The closing tale of the old woman who cannot teach the Way to someone lacking the stuff explains why Williams failed as Senators manager: his players did not have the native talent to receive it.

Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.

Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.

chapters.file: ch41 - Where in the World(s) Are We.md
chapters.relation: Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven. He concludes counterfactuals need some other explanation and that we should savor the actual Foulke-to-Mientkiewicz final out of 2004 instead.

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher whose 'Good and Evil' argues the meaning of life lies in engagement in activity itself (his Sisyphus essay), against Schopenhauerian pessimism.
holes.why: Chapter 28 builds its middle innings on Taylor's reply to Schopenhauer—endless striving is the essence of a meaningful life—as the bridge to the Nietzschean ethics of challenge.

holes.name: The Disenchantment of the World
holes.what: Horkheimer and Adorno's thesis in Dialectic of Enlightenment that Enlightenment rationality reduces the world to calculable categories, dispelling myth and meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 32 quotes 'Enlightenment's program was the disenchantment of the world' to diagnose fans reducing Johnny Damon's entire career to the single concept 'traitor'.

holes.name: A. Bartlett Giamatti
holes.what: Yale Renaissance scholar, National League president and baseball commissioner (1938–1989) who wrote philosophical essays on baseball, leisure and American culture, including 'Take Time for Paradise'.
holes.why: Chapter 36 crowns him 'the Philosopher' and builds its account of Fenway's sacredness, winning as betterment, and circular time on quotations from 'Take Time for Paradise' and 'A Great and Glorious Game'.
